counterexample: Distributivity gives ((m\vee n)\vee b) \wedge ((m\vee n)\vee a) = (m\vee n) \vee (a\wedge b), not (m\vee n)\wedge(a\vee b). In the powerset lattice of {1,2} with m\vee n = {1}, a = {2}, b = {2}: LHS = {1,2}\cap{1,2} = {1,2}, while the claimed value (m\vee n)\wedge(a\vee b) = {1}\cap{2} = \emptyset.
reasoning_summary: Steps 0001-0020 check out: m\vee(n\vee b) \ge n\vee b and n\vee b \in F give m\vee(n\vee b) \in F by upward closure of the filter (0004-0008); associativity gives (m\vee n)\vee b \in F (0012); the symmetric argument gives (m\vee n)\vee a \in F (0016); and closure of a filter under meets gives ((m\vee n)\vee b) \wedge ((n\vee m)\vee a) \in F (0020). Step 0024 then misapplies distributivity: the meet of two joins over a common element c = m\vee n distributes as (c\vee b)\wedge(c\vee a) = c \vee (a\wedge b), a join of c with the meet of a and b. The proof instead writes (m\vee n) \wedge (b\vee a), swapping both connectives, and these expressions are not equal in a distributive lattice (see counterexample). The error is load-bearing rather than cosmetic: the correct expression c\vee(a\wedge b) lands in the ideal M only via the parent theorem's hypothesis a\wedge b \in M together with closure of an ideal under joins, whereas the proof's subsequent line 0027 asserts 'by assumption b\vee a \in M', an assumption present nowhere in the statement and false in the intended setting where a,b \notin M. So the first step that certainly fails is 0024.
verdict_note: early stop at first certain failure
